# PREFACE

->To the one who reads this.<-

<image-desc>Large ornamental drop cap letter 'W' decorated with intricate floral and leaf motifs.</image-desc>

**W**e present to you here /
**Kind Reader** / the very latest
**controversies** from **Holland**.
Regarding which / before we
display the contents / we wish 
first to briefly share with you 
their beginning and progress.

The greatest curiosity / that can strike a reader here / 
is without doubt the desire to know / who 
**Moses Germanus** <note>original: *Moses Germanus* (Moses the German). This was the pseudonym of Johann Peter Spaeth (c. 1642–1701), a German theologian who converted from Catholicism to Lutheranism, then to Pietism, and finally to Judaism.</note> actually is. However / 
we have already said so much about this on the **title page** / 
that one cannot rightly expect more from us here. 
For there we have named that name / under 
which he has written various books / as is 
known to those / who are familiar with the 
**Republic of Letters**. <note>original: *Bücher-Staats*. Literally "State of Books," this refers to the scholarly world and the contemporary bibliographical records of published works.</note> It shall suffice us 
however to hear / that this **Moses Germanus**, 
who was **Catholic** by nature <note>meaning by birth or upbringing.</note> / after 
he passed through various changes of opinions and 
sects / finally here in **Amsterdam** al-
lowed himself to be **circumcised** among the 
**Portuguese**. <note>original: *Portugiesen*. This refers to the Sephardic Jewish community in Amsterdam, which was largely composed of former "New Christians" (conversos) from the Iberian Peninsula.</note> With this **M. G.** 
our author became acquainted by chance / (as 
is prone to happen while traveling) /

The Author, who had recently arrived here from **Germany** / and as a traveler <note>original: *Passagier*</note> could not easily involve himself in extensive controversies / initially showed little inclination to answer / especially since he could not yet know / whether he would be able to wait for the outcome of the dispute / or continue his journey to **England**. Therefore, he left this comparison by his countryman unanswered for a time. After several weeks had passed / and after **M. G.** had repeatedly sent reminders / urging that he should indeed answer / he finally sat down / and put his **Reflection** <note>A formal written response or philosophical critique.</note> to paper, likewise in German / and sent it to **Moses Germanus** / who afterwards provided the Reflection with another German answer / and thus one answer arose from the other / as is customary in such cases. In this manner, these two countrymen in a far-distant land by the sea / through a wondrous confluence of events / fell into combat and dispute / yet without any breach of the love and friendliness / which one human being owes to another.

However, it should be known / that **M. G.** did not wish to be bound to the comparison he had once made in this combat / but instead continually digressed into other matters / and for that reason, that specific answer / which appears on **page 31** /

Concerning the content of the disputation / it is very delicate and new / and we have no newer controversies in **Holland** than these. For there is a struggle over the nature of God / over the purpose and <term>object</term> <note>the focus or defining goal</note> of the Jewish religion / and over the world / whether it be the revealed God. One sees here, proven with astonishment (which until now one would not have believed / and will certainly cause a great sensation among many /) that the fundamental and chief doctrine of the Jews against the Christians is this: that all being is God. ...he went further / and felt it with the palm of his hand / then with his fist / though trembling / grasped it / until he finally caught it between his tightly squeezed fingers / and was himself astonished at his discovery.

From this, two parts later emerged / the first of which deals / with discovering **Spinozism** <note>The philosophy of Baruch Spinoza, which many 17th-century critics viewed as a dangerous form of atheism or pantheism</note> within **Judaism** / and the second / with refuting it within **Judaism**. Both parts have become very small and concise. The reason for this is / that one cannot easily write large and thick books while traveling / nor does one have the time or opportunity / to consult many authors / to research / and to expand the material through long digressions. Nevertheless, the Author has left nothing out / that can be said within a brief conceptual framework. In particular, the reader will be informed for their edification from this small work / (1.) that our new **Ebionites** <note>Historically an early Jewish-Christian sect; here used as a derogatory term for contemporary Christians who were adopting Jewish traditions or ideas</note>, who are half-dazed by **Judaism** / and consume their lives in the muck <note>original: "Dreck"</note> of **Rabbinic writings** / have fallen among hellish murderers / who give them a cup full of newly-invented abominations to drink instead of true and ancient **Wisdom** / and fill them with the forgetting of God instead of the knowledge of God. (2.) That in the future one must form an entirely different **Idea** <note>original Latin: "Idea," meaning a mental concept or framework</note> of **Judaism**. That our controversies with the **Jews** are quite different / than those concerning the **Messiah**. That the **Jews** have an entirely different **God** than we do. That we understand nothing of their **Old Testament**. And that / since they have turned themselves toward philosophizing / they cannot be refuted / except through the path of **Philosophy**. (3.) That the **Jewish Syna-**

**Synagogue** is indeed that **Son of Perdition** <note>A term from 2 Thessalonians 2:3, traditionally associated with the Antichrist</note> / of whom **St. Paul** prophesied / that he would exalt himself above all / that is called **God** and **divine service** / so that he will sit in the **Temple of God** / as a god / and claim that he is God / 2 Thess. 2:4. For it <note>the Synagogue/the Jewish people</note> exalts itself above all that is called God / that is, **Authorities** / in that it calls the authorities under whom it lives / a **Roman Pharaoh** / a **Roman She-wolf** <note>A derogatory reference to the legendary founder of Rome; here used to mock the Roman or secular authorities</note> and so forth. It claims / to be **God**: in that it calls itself God’s only and begotten son / indeed, God himself / and the center of all God's good qualities. (4.) That in the future one must **philosophize** quite differently / than has happened until now. The Author, to be sure, has neither the authority nor the age / to promulgate a new **philosophy** to the world. But regardless of this, he has perhaps made his thoughts not a little **plausible** <note>original: "probabel"</note> to those / who, following **Plato's** reminder, do not care so much / *who* says a thing / as *what* is being said / and who are also willing to learn from the lowly and humble (among whom he gladly counts himself in his weakness). Which the outcome will surely prove.

## REPLY
### to the response of Moses Germanus to my Reflection.

I am pleased that your holidays <note>The author likely refers to Jewish festivals such as Sukkot, given the later reference to "booths."</note>, or whatever other obstacles of your religion may have been that did not allow you to write to me sooner, have finally passed. I am satisfied with your excuse; and because I believe you, believe me in return: that I have a sincere and peaceful desire to exercise myself with you in the fear of God, and to see in love and friendliness toward which side the <term>balance</term> <note>original: *bilance*</note> of the strongest arguments will lean among us—whether I should dwell with you in the **Booths** <note>original: *Lauberhütten*; a reference to the festival of Sukkot where Jews dwell in temporary shelters</note>, or you should dwell with me in the **Christian Community**; the judgment of which shall remain free to both me and you.

However, just as you showed a particular skill in your previous letter in representing my religion, I might wish that in the progress of your thoughts you had distinguished them better from one another, and that your way of disputing were more methodical and less digressive. For you well know yourself that you have answered neither the **three main points of contention** <note>original: *Haupt-Strittigkeiten*</note>—into which I have <term>resolved</term> <note>original: *resolvirt*</note> all other <term>controversies</term> that can occur between Jews and Heathens—nor have you answered the request that I attached to the end of my Reflection (something **categorical**) which would not require a question once more. Nevertheless, I will follow you as you proceed.

It has pleased you, however, to shift the accusation of **pride** <note>original: *Hoffarth*</note>—of which I previously testified my displeasure—away from my religion, almost as if in a <term>parenthesis</term>, and onto a completely different one, which is un-

or uncreated. When He is in an uncreated or pre-worldly state, God is simply all things <note>original Latin: *Deus est omnia simpliciter*</note>. However, when there is a world, the degree or measure of Being <note>original Latin: *Entitatis*</note> is not increased; instead, God unfolds and develops Himself through emanations and outpourings from the highest to the lowest <note>original Latin: *à summis ad ima*</note>, by which the various orders and forms of created things are established. Psalm 104:29, 30: *You send forth your spirit, and they are created; you hide your face, and they are troubled.* <note>original Latin: *Emittis spiritum, & creantur, abscondis faciem, & perturbantur*</note> That is:

The Cabalists <term>Kabbalists: practitioners of a mystical school of Judaism</term> explain the origin of things from the Primal Being. They also speak of a retraction <note>original: *retraction*; a pulling back or withdrawal</note> into the first Being (*Ens*), and of a revolution <note>original: *revolution*; here meaning a cycle or turning back</note> and restoration to the initial state. It is as if they had conceived this idea in their minds: that the Primal Being, or *Ensoph*, contains all things within itself, and that the same quantity of essence always remains in the universe, whether it be in the created or uncreated state. When it is in the uncreated or pre-worldly state, then God is simply everything. # The II. Answer

## Of Moses Germanus to my Reply.

As soon as I have finished the blessing of my holy Sabbath, giving thanks to my alone-good God that He has made such a great distinction between Israel and the other peoples of the world—as great as the difference between light and darkness, between holy and unholy <note>This reflects the language of the Havdalah, the Jewish ceremony marking the end of the Sabbath, which emphasizes themes of separation and distinction.</note>—this is the first work of my hands: to serve you further in true love and loving truth regarding the remainder of your well-intentioned Reply, which the Lord may thus promote and bless. Amen.

# Dispatch of this Answer.

Your second letter in response to my **reply** <term>Reply: From the French *replique*, a formal counter-argument in a legal or theological debate.</term> has finally satisfied my expectation; not that I should praise your prayer, which I consider to be pride and sin, or approve of your scolding and slandering, at which I am horrified; but rather that you now cease to hide and conceal yourselves, and now desire that I should finally prove to you those three points (to which I have reduced all **controversies** <note>original: *Controversien*</note> that can occur between Jews and **Gentiles** <note>original: *Heyden*; in this context, it refers to Christians from a Jewish perspective, often translated as "Heathens" or "Nations."</note>, and which you have so greatly avoided). You indeed believe that we Gentiles (as you always call us by way of insult, and I—to keep it brief and to yield somewhat to your Jewish pride—will not correct extensively here) understand nothing of your falsely-renowned **Kabbalah** <note>original: *Cabala*</note> and **mystical doctrine of the law** <note>original Latin: *Mystica doctrina legis*</note>, not even a word or syllable: But you yourselves have, shortly thereafter, so forcefully **anticipated** <note>original Latin/German: *præoccupieret*; here meaning to preemptively disprove one's own position.</note> me through your own **confession** <note>original: *Confession*</note>—that you do not yet understand the Kabbalah—that I can believe nothing you say about it. 4. Many other and almost innumerable things have I felt and perceived in the depth of my **selfhood** / and I am amazed that I did not feel them before. But these few shall suffice for this time. If there is now anyone / who does not know himself / and chooses to profess himself in such darkness / that he feels nothing of the sort within / I will gladly leave him to his *skepticism* and insane insensibility / nor will I hang myself from a tree for his sake / but simply answer him with what one of *Seneca’s* friends said: *

> *I think many could have attained wisdom, had they not imagined they had already attained it, had they not concealed certain things within themselves, and had they not skipped over certain things with open eyes,* <note>original Latin: "Puto multos potuisse ad Sapientiam pervenire, nisi putassent se pervenisse, nisi quædam in se dissimulâssent, quædam apertis oculis transsiliissent."</note> that is: I hold / that many could have come to wisdom / if they had not formed the imagination / that they had already arrived there / if they had not hidden and concealed certain things within themselves / or even passed over them with open eyes.

It seems, indeed, that this unfathomable **IDEA OF GOD** <note>original: "IDEA DEI"</note>, in which everything is contained that one can think, write, or signify regarding God, is denied by some; for we have seen that a **philosopher of Germany** <note>Likely referring to the mystic Jacob Böhme (1575–1624)</note> has called God the **Eternal Nothing**, the **Primal Ground** <note>original: "Ungrund"; a Böhmean term for the absolute abyss or nothingness preceding all existence</note>, the **Nature-less Being**, etc., and the **Jewish Cabala** has likewise spoken in this way. However, it is sufficiently well known that on both sides, by **Nothing** <note>original: "Nihil"</note>, one mostly understood only the **Ein Sof** <note>original: "Ensoph"; the Infinite or Unknowable God in Jewish mysticism</note>, or the **creature-less** essence of God. And if indeed something further was hidden beneath it, it will be found below to be a **contradiction** of idolatrous people (who raise the **World-Sphere** <note>original: "Welt-Krayß"</note> onto the throne of the majesty of God).

# The 3rd ATTRIBUTE.

21. (3.) The Object of Nothing must be something **absolutely independent** <note>original: *absolutè independentes*</note>. # The 4th ATTRIBUTE.

22. (4.) The Object of Nothing must possess the highest **reality** <note>original: *Realität*</note> and the most **real entity** <note>original: *Entität*</note>. ### The 5th ATTRIBUTE.

23. (5.) The eternal Object of Nothing must be either one or none. For there is only one Object of Nothing, namely the Essence <note>original: *Wesen*</note> itself, just as there is only one abstract beauty, to which all beauties may be referred. And this essence is the universal nature of all that exists; it is the great and terrible **PAN** <note>The Greek god of nature, often used in mystical philosophy to represent the "All" or the totality of the universe.</note>, but above all else, nothing more is to be found. This same point is also proven by a contradictory absurdity <note>original: *contradictorischen absurdo*</note>. For if there were two Objects of Nothing, one could show no reason why the other would necessarily have to be essential: and thus He would have no necessary existence <note>original: *Existenz*</note>, and would immediately lack the 1st Attribute of the Object, that is, He would not be the Object. The same situation applies to even more objects. From this it follows that the great and eternal Object of the non-thing <note>original: *Unding*</note> is only one and singular. He is the *one and only substance* <note>original: *Substantia una & sola*</note>, and outside of Him there is no self-being <note>original: *Selbst-Wesen*</note>. He is one, not as the second and third numbers are one, but as the first number, in which all other numbers lie. He is the most singular unity <note>original: *Unität*</note>, and there is no division in Him; and therefore He is not distinguished from himself, nor set apart, nor divided. His special glory and privilege consist in an undivided and simple being-alone. From eternity He has no

For these things cannot pertain to the Object.

## The 1st *PERFECTION*.

29. And accordingly, the **Object of Nothing** must necessarily and primarily be something *vital* or **living**—that is to say, something self-moving and centrally-living. Where this *perfection is lacking* <note>original: *manquieret*</note>, there is an obvious **lack of being**. For what kind of perfection is that, to which the degree of **life** can still be added? Or what use is the **self-essence** <note>original: *Selbst-wesen*</note> if it is neither **life** nor **self-life**? If it must then be a **life** and a **self-life** which is to *pass* <note>original: *passiren*; to be accepted as valid</note> for the Object of Nothing, then—because this **Object** is eternal—the **life** must also be eternal; and just as He is the eternal **Ob-**

39. It must be noted, however, what the Scripture says and what *philosophy* proves: *My thoughts are not your thoughts.* Namely, the thoughts of the objective Being are very *different* from ours and from the thoughts of the entire world of spirits. The spirit-world does not make truths, but rather finds them. Its thoughts begin from the passive *intellect* <note>original: *leydenden Intelligenz*, referring to the mind as a receiver of information</note>, and are mere shadows or impressions of sensory *ideas*. It cannot think of spiritual things themselves without borrowing some *images* <note>original: *Idola* or "little pictures"</note> from the *material* or fiery world. But it is entirely different with the objective Being. It does not find truths, but rather *makes* them; and without its creative forming <note>German: *dichten*, implying both poetic creation and intentional structuring</note>, there is neither world nor truth. Its thoughts are always something creative, except when its thinking is a *conscience* or *middle knowledge* <term>middle knowledge: (Latin: *scientia media*) a theological concept where God knows all possibilities and what any free creature would do in any given situation</term>. It never thinks without its thinking being a *fabrication* of *ideas* and truths that do not yet *exist*. Indeed, it is impossible and *contradictory* for its thinking to be anything else. Since it has triumphed in solitary existence from eternity, and nothing has existed outside of it that was not from it and out of it, its thinking can be no impression nor an *idea* or *picture* borrowed from without, because outside of it there is nothing—not even a shadow or an *idea*.

He thinks what and when He wills, and His freedom determines His wisdom in thinking. In this, God is distinct from us.

### The 6th PERFECTION.

41. # The 9th ATTRIBUTE.

51. (9.) The Antithesis of Nothingness <note>original: *Gegenstand von Nichts*; literally "Object of Nothing," referring to the Divine Being as that which stands in direct opposition to non-existence</note> must be something **Immutable** according to its nature and essence / that is / according to its attributes and perfections. He must always be equal to Himself in all respects / without the alternation of light and darkness / and without the slightest transformation or change to His simplicity <term>simplicity: the theological concept that God is not made of parts, but is a single, unified essence</term>. For what could change Him or make Him **unequal**? The **Nothingness** outside of Him? But this is **nothing** / and remains **nothing** / and just as it has no essence / it likewise has no effect. He Himself? But this is impossible and contradictory. For if the eternal Antithesis of Nothingness could make Himself other than He is by the necessity of His nature / then this transformation and overturning of His essence would either have to bring Him closer to nothing <note>original: *Nihilo*</note> / or remove Him further from it / or it would have to divide Him / and then mix Him back together. A fourth possibility cannot be imagined. Now, however, He cannot approach nothingness / for He is its opposite. To move further away than He already is is also impossible. For He is **Essence** itself / and just as much as the **Non-thing** <note>original: *Unding*; a void or complete lack of being</note> excludes / He, on the contrary, includes. He cannot divide Himself either. For where He could divide Himself / He could once again approach **Nothing**. For He could then / by withdrawing His perfections / stand empty and deficient in one part / that is / cease to be the Fullness / contrary to the 6th and 7th Attribute. Furthermore, He could split apart in the middle / that is / He could cease to be **One** / which is against the **Demonstra-** <note>The word concludes on the next page as "Demonstration."</note>

<vocab>Gegenstand (Antithesis/Object), Nichts (Nothingness), Attribut (Attribute), Unveränderliches (Immutable), Wesen (Essence/Being), Unding (Non-thing), Nihilo (Nothing), Perfectionen (Perfections)</vocab>

<summary>This page argues for the immutability of God, asserting that as the absolute "Essence," He cannot be changed, divided, or moved closer to "Nothingness" by any external or internal force. The author concludes that any change in God would contradict His nature as the unified Fullness of being.</summary>

Furthermore, this second fundamental doctrine also sins against the 8th Attribute. For it severs God from Himself / and mixes Him again with Himself / and yet distinguishes Him in this composition from Himself. Before, God was everything in Himself; now He is everything in everything.

I have produced and proven the truth above; whoever wishes to look further into it and compare it with the Jewish teachings, we have already provided a heap of material for his meditations there.

### C H A P T E R  I X.

# That the present world, from top to bottom, neither *bounds* nor *modifies* anything in the Divine Unity.

59. This follows from what preceded. For if the Divine Being, by the necessity of its nature, is always <term>independent of creation</term> <note>original: *Creaturloß*; the state of God existing purely in Himself without the necessity of a created universe</note> and most strongly resists being <term>modified</term> <note>original: *modificieret*; in 17th-century philosophy, this refers to changing the "mode" or state of a substance</note>, then the world likewise can neither <term>bound</term> <note>original: *terminiren*; to set a limit or boundary to something that is otherwise infinite</note> nor modify anything in that same Being. From which it further follows that the world is something outside of God, and God is absolutely something outside of the world. For if the world were something Divine, or if it bounded anything in the Divine Being, it would have to be because the Divine Being—through itself and in itself—shows and represents all worldly things from top to bottom. But this could not then be understood without simultaneously understanding that the Divine Being changes and transforms itself (or has changed and transformed itself) into those things which we see and feel. Now, however, such a transformation and deformation of the Divine Being is impossible and <term>contradictory</term> <note>original: *contradictorisch*; logically inconsistent with the definition of God as unchanging</note>, as we have sufficiently proven above. From which it then follows that the present and visible world neither bounds nor modifies anything in the unity of the highly praised God. Which was to be demonstrated.

## CHAPTER X.

### What a great difference there is between God and the present world, taken as a whole.

60. This judgment of our **intellect** <note>original: *Verstandes*; the rational faculty used for logical discernment</note> is further strengthened and confirmed for everyone by the judgment of their **conscience**. For when we hold these two together—the **intellect** and the **gnawing conscience** <note>original: *nagende Gewissen*; the internal moral compass that "bites" or pricks the soul</note>—as is only right, and accept them as judges in the present **disputed question**, we find the difference between **God** and the present visible **world** is as great and noticeable as the difference between two **contradictions** <note>original: *Contradictionen*</note> and **opposites** <note>original: *Gegenständen*</note> can ever be. Within the **Essence of God** <note>original: *Wesen Gottes*</note> is an ever-constant and necessary **existence**. The **essence of the world**, however, lies in the alternation of **being** with **non-being**, and the one with the other. **God** is an ever-constant and present **"is"** <note>referring to the eternal present or the biblical "I Am"</note>. The **world** lies in the **succession** and **toil** <note>original: *Kwahl* (Qual); likely referring to the restless, agonizing motion of temporal life compared to divine peace</note> of the ages. **God** is neither His own cause nor **effect** <note>original: *effect*; God exists beyond the chain of causality that governs the physical world</note>. In the **world**, one being produces another. **God** is the highest **reality** <note>original: *Realität*</note>, and there is no **illusory being** <note>original: *Scheinwesen*</note> in Him. The **world** is full of fleeting **forms**, **accidents** <note>original: *Accidentien*; in philosophy, properties that can change without altering the core essence of a thing</note>, and such things that one calls **qualities** <note>original: *Qualitates*</note>, but which one might better call empty **affections** <note>original: *Afficientien*; external influences or modes of being</note> and **appearances** <note>original: *Apparentien*</note>. In **God** there is no **multiplicity** <note>original: *Vielheit*; the state of being many or composed of parts</note>. The **world** is full of **numbers**.

The sap that the tree draws into itself takes on the nature of an apple at the top, and the **nourishments** <note>original: *Alimenten*</note> we consume transform into our flesh and blood, and so forth. It is shaped, mixed, and assembled in a hundred thousand different ways. Whoever wishes to meditate upon this finds an infinity before him that he shall not exhaust in his lifetime. These are, in general, the **differences** <note>original Latin: *Differentien*</note> between God and the material world.

->Tafel<-

## How great a difference there is between God and the present world of fire.

66. This conscience dictates to our pen such a definition of fire: Fire is a **Central Nature** / that is, a nature that possesses a few perfections within an atomic and immaterial, yet extensible center. <note>original: *ausdähnlich*—referring to the philosophical concept of "extension," the property of taking up space or being stretched out.</note> These perfections include liveliness / activity / luminosity / fruitfulness / speed / penetrability / the art of painting / the art of modeling <note>original: *Poussier-kunst*—the decorative art of modeling shapes in wax, plaster, or clay; here used figuratively for how fire shapes the material world.</note> and elastic power / and it is also able to externalize these same qualities. But this self-motion is in the center in a state of sleep: it cannot come forth when it wishes / for there is no *arbitrium* <note>original: *Arbitrium*—Latin for the power of choice or free will.</note> in it / but rather, where it is to manifest itself / it must first be awakened by a foreign motion. Its power is something astonishing / I confess it; but there is nonetheless no omnipotence in it to create a world / for example, a **spirit-world**. And although it can perhaps bring forth a **material-world** as a miscarriage / <note>original: *abortiren*—to miscarry or bring forth prematurely; suggests the material world is an imperfect, flawed creation compared to the divine.</note> it nonetheless cannot create a riddle of nature / nor direct everything toward a certain final purpose; for there is no wisdom in it to devise such things / even if there were power in it to carry them out. Accordingly, the fire-world does not work what it wills / but—

### CHAPTER XIII.

## What a great difference there is between **GOD** and **ME**, I who belong to the **SPIRIT-WORLD**.

68. For this time, I will measure others by my own yardstick. <note>original: *meiner Ellen*; literally "my own ell," a traditional unit of measurement. The author is saying he will use his own self-examination as a standard for understanding all spirits.</note> For where I am distinct from God, then certainly the entire spirit-world—which has the very same conscience and the very same experience that I have—must be distinct from God. Or, let someone name for me a person who, in the examination of themselves, has found it otherwise and felt it differently than I presently feel.

I feel, however, thus:

(1.) I see no reason <note>original: *raison*; the author uses the French/Latin term common in 17th-century philosophical German.</note> why I must be necessary, for I am neither infinite <note>original: *infinit*; Latinate term for "unbounded."</note> in essence, nor have I existed from eternity. I am not infinite in essence. For I am sufficiently aware of my weaknesses and deficiencies. I have also not existed from eternity. For if I had been from eternity, then I would be the eternal thing. <note>In the philosophy of this period, "the eternal thing" or *Ens Aeternum* refers to a being that exists by its own necessity—God.</note>

But now, I was born only 26 years ago and came into this world. And even if human testimonies <note>This likely refers to birth records or the accounts of his parents.</note> were to deceive me, I still know for certain that I only recently began to reflect <note>original: *reflectiren*; to turn one's thoughts inward upon the self.</note> upon myself. It may be that I existed before I came into this world, and that I have forgotten it. I do not argue against that. <note>This is a nod to the concept of the "pre-existence of souls," an idea famously held by Plato and some mystical Christian thinkers.</note> But that I should be the **Eternal** itself, about that...

<summary>The author uses his own life—specifically his 26 years of age and his awareness of personal flaws—to argue that humans (and all spirits) are distinct from the infinite and eternal nature of God. He acknowledges the possibility of the soul's existence before birth but distinguishes such a state from being truly "eternal" in the divine sense.</summary>

What are we humans? A **philosopher** <note>original: *Philosophus*; likely referring to Aristotle or the Scholastic tradition.</note> says based on his art: **man is a rational animal** <note>original: *homo est Animal rationale*</note>; man is a creature endowed with reason. This is how we humans measure ourselves against the swine. But what is man before and compared to **God**, and compared to the **angels**? It is true: compared to lions and swine, man is a higher and better animal. We leave that definition to the **pagan philosophers** and the other scholars in the schools. But according to **Theology**, we must measure man against God, and thus say: God is eternal, righteous, holy, truthful, and in **summary**, God is all goodness. In contrast, however, man is mortal, unrighteous, deceitful, full of vice, sin, and wickedness. With God is all goodness; with man is death, the devil, and hellish fire. God is from eternity and remains in eternity. Man is mired in sin and lives in the midst of death at every moment. That is man compared to God.

### CHAPTER XIV.

## That the present world from top to bottom is an Un-god. <note>The author uses the term *Ungott* (Un-god) to argue that the physical world is essentially non-divine and should not be confused with the nature of God Himself.</note>

74. **T**his conclusion follows quite correctly from the preceding chapters. For if God, by the necessity of His nature, is creature-less <note>original: *creaturloß*; meaning God’s existence is self-sufficient and does not require the existence of any created thing.</note> / according to Chapter 7; and the present world defines nothing in the Divine Unity / according to Chapter 9. If, furthermore, a truly contradictory inequality between **God** and the **World**—whether taken as a whole or divided into its parts—is found / according to Chapters 10, 11, 12, and 13. Then the world must necessarily be an **Un-god** from top to bottom / and it must be false / what is said / that all being is **God** / that outside of the intellect nothing exists in the world but **Divine** essence / i.e., **Divine** *attributes* <note>original: *Attributa*; a reference to the philosophical properties of a substance.</note> and *modes* <note>original: *modi*; the specific forms or appearances that attributes take.</note> of the attributes / that the world constitutes the created state of **God** / that the world is the **Primal Being** <term>Urwesen: The original, fundamental essence or primary source of all existence.</term> in a *dependent* <note>original: *dependente*</note> manner / that the world is the small and sensitive object of the light / and so forth.

# CHAPTER XV.

## That God is Something Outside the World.

75. **A**ll that has been said up to this point aims toward this conclusion / and there is no chapter discussed above that does not contribute a particular force <note>original: *force*; meaning logical weight or argumentative strength</note> to this. If the present world neither limits <note>original: *terminiret*</note> nor modifies <note>original: *modifiret*</note> anything in the substance <term>Substanz: The fundamental, unchanging reality of a thing, as opposed to its outward appearance.</term> or extension <term>Ausdehnung: The property of taking up space; the author argues God does not occupy space like physical matter does.</term> of God / but is so utterly unlike God that one may call it the embodied Un-god / according to the preceding Chapter 14. Then the consequence follows correctly / that God / just as He is the opposite <note>original: *Gegenstand*; here used in the sense of a counterpart or opposing entity</note> of Nothingness / must also be the opposite of the world / that neither God is in the world / nor the world in God / that each is in itself / God in Himself / and the world in itself / that God, from top to bottom, exhibits <note>original: *exhibire*</note>, represents <note>original: *repræsentire*</note>, or works <note>original: *würcke*</note> nothing in the world through Himself except within Himself / that He is by no means **WHOLLY** in all beings and parts of beings / and parts of particles / nor is He the **INNERMOST** in all things / and in the effects of things: But rather that He is entirely something outside the world / supernatural / and non-creaturely / I will say/

...to that turbid matter. So that nothing at all is found in this world in which there is not something spiritual and vital, according to the proportion of its corporeity and materiality, and according to the degree of its distance from the source and quarry <note>original Latin: *latomia*; literally a stone-quarry, used here metaphorically as the "bedrock" or origin of all substances</note> of all things, etc.

That is: There is nothing in the world to which something of the upper light does not flow. However, this influx of light is always distinct according to the difference of its descent from the higher to the lower—which, in consideration of even lower levels, is itself an "upper" level. And so these streams of light thicken and become embodied from degree to degree, just as it happens to this turbid matter. Thus, nothing in this world can be pointed out in which there is not something spiritual and living, according to the mass of its embodiment and thickening, and according to the degrees of its distance from the highest origin and outflow of all things. 

They know no other way to explain this thickening of corporeal things than through a diminishing of light—that is, through a **privation** <note>original: *Privation*; in philosophical terms, a "privation" is the absence or lack of a quality that should naturally be present. Here, matter is seen as the "lack" of full divine light</note>. Therefore, this same Rabbi explains the entire mystery in that place by using the analogy of a **lamp** which is set up in a large church; its rays are indeed bright and clear at the source, but the further they reach, the longer and weaker they become, until one can finally hardly see one another in the furthest corners. 

In this way, matter is to them nothing other than a **most thin light** <note>original Latin: *tenuissima lux*</note>, that is, a dark material of the Divine substance, and an almost extinguished coal. From this, one sees that they do not absolutely deny the existence of matter, but merely define it as a privation. For that which is darkened in God is, to them, the very essence of the material.

## The True Contrast Between the Christian and Jewish Religions.

Christianity <note>original: *Christenthumb*. An archaic spelling of *Christentum*.</note> is a form of piety that has as its goal and object <note>original: *Vorwurff*. In this period, the word meant "object of focus" or "subject matter" rather than its modern meaning of "reproach."</note> the otherworldly and hidden nature of God—the eternal, great, wise, and holy Being—and, through the denial of oneself and the present world, it strives in and of itself, according to its very essence <note>original: *Esse*. Latin for "being" or "existence."</note>, toward humility.

<column-break/>

Judaism <note>original: *Jüdenthumb*.</note> is a contradictory mess <note>original: *Quarck*. Literally "curds," used here as a derogatory term for nonsense or something of no value.</note> mixed together from religion and atheism, which has as its goal and object the present nature and creation—the temporal, small, foolish, and carnal existence—and, through the deification of itself and the world, it strives in and of itself, according to its very essence <note>original: *Esse*.</note>, toward all sins, and especially toward pride <note>original: *Hoffarth*. Arrogance or haughty behavior.</note>.

## DEFINITIONS.

**I. I understand by <term>Cause of itself</term> <note>original: *Caussam sui*</note> (by the self-being <note>original: *Selbstwesen*</note>) that whose essence <note>original: *Essenz*</note> involves existence <note>original: *Existenz*</note>, or that whose nature cannot be conceived except as existing.**

104. We cannot pass judgment on this definition until we first know what meaning <note>original: *Verstand*</note> it holds. Every person, however, is the best interpreter of their own understanding; and therefore we must here accept the words in the interpretation that is pleasing to the Author <note>Spinoza</note>. Now, it is pleasing to the Author that we make a distinction between "to exist" and "to involve existence." He calls that "involving existence" which cannot be conceived as non-existing. Conversely, what can be conceived as non-existing (such as, for example, all things created and produced by God), he denies that it "involves existence," even though it actually exists. This is how he explains himself in Axiom 7: <gloss>What can be conceived as non-existing, its essence does not include existence.</gloss> He does not deny that it exists or can exist, but rather that it "involves existence." Furthermore, he calls "involving existence" that which exists through the necessity of its nature, which is uncreated and unproduced, which is the cause of its own existence, and which maintains itself in an always-equal existence and duration; in short, to its—

105. It is difficult and nearly impossible to discover how the *Author* <note>Spinoza</note> understood this description. All the words here suffer from a double interpretation, and the *Author* has interpreted them now one way, now another, as his interests required. *Being in itself* is spoken of in two ways. That is already "in itself" which is not in another, e.g., **extension** <note>original: *Ausdähnung*; the physical property of occupying space</note>. The same is also called "in itself" when the cause of its existence is within its nature and description. Thus, the <term>Self-being</term> <note>original: *Selbſtweſen*; the ultimate, independent reality or God</note> is in itself. For *being* belongs to its nature, and the cause of its *being* is not found outside of it. *To be conceived through itself* is also <term>double-tongued</term> <note>original: *zweyzungicht*; meaning ambiguous or capable of two meanings</note>. Something can be called "conceivable through itself" insofar as its concept does not require the concept of another thing, such as, for example, *extension* without *motion*, or the **Fire-World** <note>original: *Feür-Welt*; likely a reference to a specific cosmological realm or element in 17th-century physics</note> without

In mathematics <note>original: *Mathesi*</note>, one calls a **figure** **that which is enclosed by one or more boundaries.** This *definition* is good, for it expresses nothing more than the *simple* nature of the thing. **VI.** By God, I understand an **absolutely** infinite thing, that is, a **substance** consisting of infinite **attributes**, each of which expresses an eternal and infinite **essence**.

### EXPLANATION.

I say that God is absolutely infinite, not merely infinite in its kind; for regarding that which is only infinite in its kind, infinite **attributes** can be denied. But to the essence of that which is **absolutely** infinite belongs everything that expresses an essence and does not involve the **reason** <note>original: *Ration*</note> of non-being.

## The 1st Proposition.

### Substance is by nature prior to its affections. <note>Spinoza defines "affections" (or modes) as the specific qualities or states that exist within a substance, like a thought within a mind.</note>

This is evident from the 3rd and 5th <term>Definitions</term>.

112. If substance means the same as essence or natural matter, then the proposition is unfailing. But if substance means the same as self-being or <term>cause of itself</term> <note>original Latin: *Causa sui*; the idea that something’s own nature is the reason it exists</note>, then it is just as absurd as if I were to say: parallel lines exist before the obtuse angles where they meet. # The 1st **Corollary**. <note>original: "Corollarium"</note>

From this it follows quite clearly (1.) that there is only one God / that is, according to the 6th **Definition** <note>original: "Defin."</note>, that in the nature of things, only one single **substance** <note>original: "Substanz"</note> is given, and that it is **absolutely infinite** <note>original: "absolut infinit"</note>.

122. If **substance** is **assumed** <note>original: "supponiret"</note> here to mean **cause of itself** <term>Causa sui: a philosophical concept referring to something that brings itself into being and depends on nothing else for its existence</term>, then the conclusion is correct: since besides God no **cause of itself** can be either found or understood, God must be unique, or rather only one **cause of itself** is given, which is God, the infinite one. Although it is then denied that in the nature of things which we see and feel, there is that same single substance—which has not yet been proven. But if **substance** is **assumed** to mean every material <note>original: "Stoff"</note> in which a nature resides, and many such materials can be given and **conceived** <note>original: "conci-piert"</note> outside of God—as was **observed** <note>original: "observiret"</note> regarding the previous **proposition** <note>original: "PropositionReference"</note>—then the corollary vanishes of its own accord. For (1.) from the fact that many materials are given and can be conceived outside of God, it does not follow that God's prerogative consists in being alone. Even less (2.) that in the nature of things only a single material is given; and least of all (3.) that this same material is **absolutely** <note>original: "absolut"</note> infinite, the **cause of itself**, or God Himself.

## The 2nd **Corollary**. <note>original: "Corollarium"</note>

It follows (2.) that extended and thinking things are either attributes of God, or, according to the 1st **Axiom** <note>original: "Axioma"</note>, **affections** <term>Affections: in 17th-century philosophy, these are the modes or specific "states" of a substance—how it is modified or expressed</term> of the Divine attributes.

123. Simply because many **substances** <note>original: "Stoffen"</note> can exist outside of God which are not God, it does not follow at all that the **extension** <term>Extension: the property of taking up physical space; one of the two attributes of reality defined by Spinoza</term> or the thinking thing found in those same substances outside of God must be God's attributes or affections of His attributes. Rather, purely the opposite follows: namely, that they are neither attributes of God nor affections of His attributes. At most, this follows: that the attributes of those substances outside of God must necessarily be explained through an **attribute of God** <note>original: "Attributum Dei"</note>, because God is a being of infinite attributes, of whom all **realities** <note>original: "Realitäten"</note>—which do not involve the **reason** <note>original: "Ration"</note> of non-being—and thus all **perfections** <note>original: "Perfectionen"</note> of **creatures** <note>original: "Creaturen"</note> must be affirmed. This does not belong here, and it is not what the author intends with his **corollary**.

## The 15th **Proposition**. <note>original: "Proposition"</note>

Everything that exists is in God, and without God, nothing can be **conceived** <note>original: "begriffen"</note>.

# PROOF. <note>original: "BEWEIS"</note>

Aside from **God**, there is no **substance** <term>Substance: in 17th-century philosophy, this refers to something that exists independently and does not need anything else to be understood</term>, nor can any be **conceived** <note>original: "concipiert"</note> / according to the 14th **Proposition**. That is: Aside from **God**, there is no thing that is in itself / and can be understood through itself / according to the 3rd **Definition**. The **modes** <term>Modes: the specific forms, qualities, or "states" that a substance takes; for example, a specific thought is a mode of the attribute of Thought</term>, however, according to the 5th **Definition**, can neither exist nor be understood without the **substance**; therefore, they must exist in the **Divine nature** alone / and be understood through it alone. Now, however, there is absolutely nothing aside from the **substance** and its **modes**, according to the 1st **Axiom** <term>Axiom: a self-evident truth used as a starting point for a logical argument</term>. Therefore, nothing can exist without **God**, nor can it be understood.

124. This **proposition** and its **proof** rest upon mere falsehoods / the lack of foundation of which has already been shown frequently, even to the point of nausea <note>original: "biß auff den Eckel"</note>. That there is no **substance** aside from **God** / nor that one can be **conceived** / is the falsity of the preceding **proposition**. That there exists a thing aside from **God** which is in itself / and can be understood through itself / has been sufficiently observed regarding **Definition 3** and **Axiom 1**. That the **modes** aside from the **substance** (insofar as the word **substance** is dedicated to **God** / and signifies the **cause of itself** <note>original: "Causam sui"</note>) not only can / but must also exist and be understood / has been noted regarding the 5th **Definition**. # The 16th *Proposition*.

From the necessity of the Divine *Nature*, infinite things must follow in infinite ways—I mean to say, everything that can fall within an infinite *intellect*—must follow.

## *PROOF*.

This *Proposition* must be obvious to anyone who will only pay attention to the fact that the *intellect concludes* from the *definition* of any thing those properties which truly follow from the *nature* of that same thing; and it does so all the more, the more *realities* the *definition* expresses, or the more the essence of the described thing involves. We see that in **geometrical principles** <term>Geometriſchen Principien: the fundamental laws and axioms of geometry</term>, endless things must lie hidden—that is to say, arts, truths, inventions, and so forth—nonetheless, we can perceive only the smallest part of them. Therefore, not everything, nor infinite things, nor things in infinite ways, follow from the nature of God into **externalization**, but only that which God is pleased to **externalize** and reveal.

But it is enough that in his **definition** <note>Referring to Spinoza's Definition 6 of God as an absolutely infinite being</note>, nothing can be pointed out from which one could conclude that infinite things must actually follow from His nature in infinite ways, just as one can conclude from the **definition** of the **circle** <note>original: *Zirckels*</note> that all lines drawn from the **center** <note>original: *Centro*</note> to the **circumference** <note>original: *Umblauff*</note> must be equal to one another. is not pleasing to the Author <note>The "Author" refers to Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), whose *Tractatus Politicus* is being critiqued here.</note>. For he insists that sin belongs to the nature and definition of man, and that man can neither exist nor be understood without it. Accordingly, he recognizes no distinction between those impulses that arise in us from reason and those that arise from other causes; rather, he considers them all to be forces of nature and natural effects through which human nature expresses itself, likewise as endeavors through which man seeks to preserve himself. Thus, to him, so-called <term>original sin</term> <note>The Christian doctrine that all humans are born with a built-in urge to do wrong, inherited from Adam.</note> is a utopian *chimera* <note>original Latin: *Chimæra*; a mythical beast made of mismatched parts, used here to mean an impossible or fabricated idea.</note>. According to this, he subsequently recognizes no <term>actual sin</term> <note>German: *thätliche Sünde*; specific sinful acts committed by an individual, as opposed to the state of original sin.</note>.

For he supposes that all human actions take their origin from the necessity of the Divine nature, and therefore belong to the ordinance of God in nature and creation, and thus cannot possibly be sin, Chapter 2, number 18. He supposes that man always acts—whether he acts through the impulse of reason or of blind desires—according to the law and rules of nature, and acts according to the right of nature, in the same place <note>original Latin: *ibid.*, short for *ibidem*; referring to the previously cited Chapter 2 of Spinoza's work.</note>, number 5. Thereafter, he flatly denies that man is obligated to live according to reason. For if he were so obligated by the ordinance of nature, he would necessarily have to live that way in fact, because the ordinance of nature is that which necessarily follows from the nature of God. 

But now men are mostly governed by irrationality. From this he then concludes that it is not ordained by God in nature and creation to live according to the impulse of reason, and that there is absolutely <note>original Latin: *absolutè*</note> no sin against the law of nature. See Chapter 2, number 18. He admits, to be sure, that men, according to human

This shall be enough for this time. I take my hand from the table and let every honest heart judge for itself whether Spinoza’s piety is anything more than pure **atheism** <note>original: "Atheisterey"</note>. Would to God that the Jews would wake up at last and recognize themselves, to see what "pretty" consequences lie hidden in the nature of their doctrine.
